claim: Mice lacking Tgfbr2 in stratified epithelia expressing Keratin 14 (K14) develop spontaneous squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) at the transition zone between the anal canal and rectum.
source: Mice lacking Tgfbr2 in stratified epithelia expressing Keratin 14 (K14) develop spontaneous squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) at the transition zone between the anal canal and rectum (Guasch et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Guasch et al., 2007

claim: All YFP+SCC cells located at the tumor–stroma interface expressed high levels of the hemidesmosomal α6 integrin.
source: Immunofluorescence staining revealed that all YFP+SCC cells located at the tumor–stroma interface expressed high levels of the hemidesmosomal α6 integrin (Figure 1D)
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1D

claim: All YFP+SCC cells located at the tumor–stroma interface expressed high levels of the focal adhesion marker β1 integrin.
source: Immunofluorescence staining revealed that all YFP+SCC cells located at the tumor–stroma interface expressed high levels of the hemidesmosomal α6 integrin (Figure 1D) and the focal adhesion marker β1 integrin (Figure 1E)
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1E

claim: A fraction of YFP+SCC cells at the tumor-stroma interface expressed CD34.
source: Immunofluorescence staining revealed that all YFP+SCC cells located at the tumor–stroma interface expressed high levels of the hemidesmosomal α6 integrin (Figure 1D) and the focal adhesion marker β1 integrin (Figure 1E), and a fraction of these expressed CD34 (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1F

claim: The frequency of epithelial CD34+ cells within the tumor varied between mice, from 7% to 34%.
source: The frequency of epithelial CD34+ cells within the tumor varied between mice, from 7% to 34%.
evidence: Supported by FACS analysis data

claim: CD34− colonies appeared to be differentiated paraclones and were unable to be passed more than once.
source: When plated on a feeder layer of irradiated fibroblasts, both YFP+CD34−and YFP+CD34+ cells sorted from Tgfbr2 cKO SCC formed colonies; however, CD34− colonies appeared to be differentiated paraclones and were unable to be passed more than once
evidence: Supported by in vitro colony formation assays

claim: CD34+ colonies appeared to form holoclones, were able to proliferate extensively, and survived unlimited passage.
source: When plated on a feeder layer of irradiated fibroblasts, both YFP+CD34−and YFP+CD34+ cells sorted from Tgfbr2 cKO SCC formed colonies; however, CD34− colonies appeared to be differentiated paraclones and were unable to be passed more than once, whereas CD34+ colonies appeared to form holoclones, were able to proliferate extensively, and survived unlimited passage (Figure 1H–I).
evidence: Supported by in vitro colony formation assays shown in Figure 1H-I

claim: CD34+ SCC cells did not respond to TGFβ stimulation, confirming the loss of TGFβRII.
source: CD34+ SCC cells did not respond to TGFβ stimulation, confirming the loss of TGFβRII, and aberrantly expressed Keratin 8, a hallmark of SCC (Ikeda et al., 2008), compared to keratinocytes isolated from the anal canal of wild-type mice (Figure 1J).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data in Figure 1J showing lack of pSMAD2 response to TGFβ treatment

claim: CD34+ SCC cells aberrantly expressed Keratin 8, a hallmark of SCC.
source: CD34+ SCC cells did not respond to TGFβ stimulation, confirming the loss of TGFβRII, and aberrantly expressed Keratin 8, a hallmark of SCC (Ikeda et al., 2008), compared to keratinocytes isolated from the anal canal of wild-type mice (Figure 1J).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data in Figure 1J and citation to Ikeda et al., 2008

claim: Orthotopic injection of 200–10^6 CD34+ cells from Tgfbr2 cKO anorectal SCC into recipient Nu/Nu mice caused secondary tumor formation with 100% efficiency (n = 89).
source: Orthotopic injection of 200–106 CD34+ cells from Tgfbr2 cKO anorectal SCC into recipient Nu/Nu mice caused secondary tumor formation with 100% efficiency (n = 89) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by orthotopic transplantation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A

claim: Secondary anorectal tumors were invasive, moderately- to poorly-differentiated SCC, characterized by cellular atypia, squamous nests with keratin pearls, intercellular bridges, aberrant mitoses, cellular disorganization and desmoplastic stroma.
source: These secondary anorectal tumors were invasive, moderately- to poorly-differentiated SCC, characterized by cellular atypia, squamous nests with keratin pearls, intercellular bridges, aberrant mitoses, cellular disorganization and desmoplastic stroma (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: Supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C

claim: Secondary tumors were morphologically similar to the primary Tgfbr2 cKO tumors of origin.
source: These secondary anorectal tumors were invasive, moderately- to poorly-differentiated SCC, characterized by cellular atypia, squamous nests with keratin pearls, intercellular bridges, aberrant mitoses, cellular disorganization and desmoplastic stroma (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), and were morphologically similar to the primary Tgfbr2 cKO tumors of origin.
evidence: Based on comparison of histological features

claim: The frequency of epithelial CD34+ cells in the secondary tumors ranged from 7% to 22%.
source: The frequency of epithelial CD34+ cells in the secondary tumors ranged from 7% to 22%.
evidence: Supported by FACS analysis data

claim: Loss of Tgfbr2 was maintained in YFP+ SCC cells in secondary tumors.
source: We confirmed that loss of Tgfbr2 was maintained in YFP+ SCC cells by qPCR (Figure 2D) and immunofluorescence staining
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 2D and immunofluorescence staining

claim: TGFβRII and nuclear pSMAD2 were still present in the surrounding stroma of secondary tumors.
source: We confirmed that loss of Tgfbr2 was maintained in YFP+ SCC cells by qPCR (Figure 2D) and immunofluorescence staining, whereas TGFβRII and nuclear pSMAD2 were still present in the surrounding stroma (Figure 2E–F).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2E-F

claim: After tertiary transplant of CD34+ SCC cells, 8/13 mice developed anorectal tumors, compared to 1 mouse of 13 transplanted with CD34− SCC cells.
source: After tertiary transplant of CD34+ SCC cells, 8/13 mice developed anorectal tumors, compared to 1 mouse of 13 transplanted with CD34− SCC cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by tertiary transplantation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B

claim: YFP+ cells negative for α6-integrin and β1-integrin were unable to form tumors upon transplantation (n = 14).
source: YFP+ cells negative for α6-integrin and β1-integrin were unable to form tumors upon transplantation (n = 14)
evidence: Supported by transplantation assay data

claim: Tertiary anorectal tumors maintained the tumor hierarchy of the primary and secondary Tgfbr2 cKO SCC.
source: Tertiary anorectal tumors maintained the tumor hierarchy of the primary and secondary Tgfbr2 cKO SCC, and selection for CD34+ CSCs resulted in an increased ratio of CD34+ cells (75%) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: Supported by FACS analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D-E

claim: In the single tertiary tumor that formed after transplant of CD34− SCC cells, CD34 was re-expressed in 49% of YFP+ epithelial tumor cells by FACS.
source: In fact, in the single tertiary tumor that formed after transplant of CD34− SCC cells, CD34 was re-expressed in 49% of YFP+ epithelial tumor cells by FACS (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G)
evidence: Supported by FACS data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G

claim: CD34 expression is dynamic in vivo in Tgfbr2-deficient SCC.
source: In fact, in the single tertiary tumor that formed after transplant of CD34− SCC cells, CD34 was re-expressed in 49% of YFP+ epithelial tumor cells by FACS (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G), indicating that CD34 expression is dynamic in vivo.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that CD34− cells can give rise to CD34+ cells

claim: Tgfbr2 cKO SCC spontaneously metastasized to the lungs with 100% frequency (n > 30 mice analyzed).
source: We analyzed the lungs of tumor-bearing mice and observed that Tgfbr2 cKO SCC indeed spontaneously metastasized to the lungs with 100% frequency (n > 30 mice analyzed) (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis of lungs shown in Figure 3A

claim: Tgfbr2 cKO lung metastases expressed Keratin 5, indicating their squamous epithelial origin.
source: These lung metastases expressed Keratin 5 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), indicating their squamous epithelial origin.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Tgfbr2 cKO lung metastases expressed YFP and contained populations of CD34+ cells.
source: Furthermore, Tgfbr2 cKO lung metastases expressed YFP and contained populations of CD34+ cells (Figure 3B–C), recapitulating the hierarchy of the primary tumor of origin.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3B-C

claim: CD34+ SCC cells were enriched for an invasive and metastatic gene signature.
source: Sequencing of RNA from CD34+ and CD34- Tgfbr2 cKO SCC cells, isolated by FACS as described in Figure 2C, revealed that CD34+ SCC cells were enriched for an invasive and metastatic gene signature as well as for mRNA involved in the RAC/RHO/RAS pathway (Figure 3D and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 3D and Supplementary file 1

claim: CD34+ SCC cells were enriched for mRNA involved in the RAC/RHO/RAS pathway.
source: Sequencing of RNA from CD34+ and CD34- Tgfbr2 cKO SCC cells, isolated by FACS as described in Figure 2C, revealed that CD34+ SCC cells were enriched for an invasive and metastatic gene signature as well as for mRNA involved in the RAC/RHO/RAS pathway (Figure 3D and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 3D and Supplementary file 1

claim: A number of genes were commonly overexpressed in Tgfbr2 deficient CD34+ anorectal transitional SCC cells and published datasets of aggressive human cancers including cervical carcinoma.
source: Using ToppCluster to generate a network of genes shared between Tgfbr2 deficient CD34+ anorectal transitional SCC cells and published datasets of aggressive human cancers (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) we found that a number of genes were commonly overexpressed in human cancers including cervical carcinoma.
evidence: Supported by bioinformatics analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: Cathepsin S, Fibrillin1, Spp1, Mmp9 and Tgfb2 are upregulated in CD34+ SCC cells and are implicated in ECM organization, invasion and metastasis.
source: We validated a selection of the most upregulated genes in the CD34+ SCC cells by qPCR (Figure 3E), including Cathepsin S, Fibrillin1, Spp1, Mmp9 and Tgfb2, which are all implicated in ECM organization, invasion and metastasis
evidence: Supported by qPCR validation shown in Figure 3E and known functions of these genes

claim: Rac2, Rhoh, RhoJ, Vav1, Dock2, and Elmo1 are upregulated in CD34+ SCC cells and are members of the RHO GTPase pathway.
source: We validated a selection of the most upregulated genes in the CD34+ SCC cells by qPCR (Figure 3E), including Cathepsin S, Fibrillin1, Spp1, Mmp9 and Tgfb2, which are all implicated in ECM organization, invasion and metastasis, and members of the RHO GTPase pathway Rac2, Rhoh, RhoJ, Vav1, Dock2, and Elmo1.
evidence: Supported by qPCR validation shown in Figure 3E

claim: The GEF ELMO1 is co-expressed with CD34-positive tumor epithelial cells at the protein level.
source: We confirmed that the GEF ELMO1 is co-expressed with CD34-positive tumor epithelial cells at the protein level by immunofluorescence staining (Figure 4A)
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A

claim: ELMO1 shows increased staining at the leading edge of the tumor.
source: We confirmed that the GEF ELMO1 is co-expressed with CD34-positive tumor epithelial cells at the protein level by immunofluorescence staining (Figure 4A) and observed increased staining of this RAC-activating factor at the leading edge of the tumor.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A

claim: RAC2 is co-expressed with CD34-positive cells.
source: We also confirmed that RAC2 is co-expressed with CD34-positive cells (Figure 4B)
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4B

claim: RAC1 is strongly expressed at the tumor-stroma border of Tgfbr2 cKO SCC.
source: We also confirmed that RAC2 is co-expressed with CD34-positive cells (Figure 4B) and that RAC1 is strongly expressed at the tumor-stroma border of Tgfbr2 cKO SCC (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4C

claim: A strong RAC activity was confirmed in vitro in Tgfbr2 cKO SCC CD34+ cells.
source: A strong RAC activity was confirmed in vitro when we analyzed the amount of GTP-bound RAC in Tgfbr2 cKO SCC CD34+ cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by RAC activity assay shown in Figure 4D

claim: RAC1 protein activity may be elevated in CSCs by upregulation of GEFs.
source: These results indicate that, while Rac1 mRNA was not found to be upregulated in CD34+ cells by RNA-Seq analysis, RAC1 protein activity may be elevated in CSCs by upregulation of GEFs.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that RAC1 protein is highly expressed and active despite no change in mRNA levels

claim: Only six genes were common between the CSC from Tgfbr2 cKO anorectal CD34+ cells and DMBA-induced Tgfbr2 cKO skin CD34Hi population (p value=1.57×10−7).
source: Bioinformatics analysis revealed that only six genes were common between the CSC from Tgfbr2 cKO anorectal CD34+ cells and DMBA-induced Tgfbr2 cKO skin CD34Hi population (***p value=1.57×10−7)
evidence: Supported by bioinformatics analysis comparing gene expression datasets

claim: Seven genes were common between Tgfbr2 cKO anorectal CD34+ cells and DMBA-induced Tgfbr2 cKO skin CD34Lo population (p value=7.48×10−5).
source: Bioinformatics analysis revealed that only six genes were common between the CSC from Tgfbr2 cKO anorectal CD34+ cells and DMBA-induced Tgfbr2 cKO skin CD34Hi population (***p value=1.57×10−7) and seven genes were common in the DMBA-induced Tgfbr2 cKO skin CD34Lopopulation (***p value=7.48×10−5) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by bioinformatics analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: The common genes between Tgfbr2 cKO anorectal CD34+ cells and DMBA-induced Tgfbr2 cKO skin CSCs are involved in ECM organization, epithelial to mesenchymal transition (EMT) and metastasis but none was related to the RAC/RHO/RAS pathway.
source: As expected in malignant cancers, these genes are involved in ECM organization, epithelial to mesenchymal transition (EMT) and metastasis but none was related to the RAC/RHO/RAS pathway.
evidence: Based on functional annotation of the common genes identified

claim: TGFβ-deficient DMBA-induced skin SCC does not express RAC1 and RAC2 in contrast to anorectal SCC, where these proteins are found at the invasive front of the tumor.
source: Immunofluorescence staining confirmed that TGFβ-deficient DMBA-induced skin SCC does not express RAC1 and RAC2 in contrast to anorectal SCC, where these proteins are found at the invasive front of the tumor (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5

claim: Aberrant RAC signaling may be a hallmark of highly aggressive tumors arising spontaneously in tumor-prone transition zones.
source: These analyses suggest that aberrant RAC signaling may be a hallmark of highly aggressive tumors arising spontaneously in tumor-prone transition zones.
evidence: Inferred from the comparison of gene expression profiles and protein expression between transition zone and skin tumors

claim: The Elmo1 promoter contains one TIE located 902 bp upstream of the TSS and one SBE located 153 bp upstream of the TSS.
source: The Elmo1 promoter contained one TIE located 902 bp upstream of the TSS and one SBE located 153 bp upstream of the TSS (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by promoter analysis shown in Figure 6A

claim: SMAD3 bound to the TIE on the Elmo1 promoter, but not to the SBE.
source: SMAD3 bound to the TIE on the Elmo1 promoter, but not to the SBE (Figure 6B)
evidence: Supported by chromatin immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6B

claim: SMAD3 did not bind to any of the sites identified on the Dock2 promoter.
source: SMAD3 bound to the TIE on the Elmo1 promoter, but not to the SBE (Figure 6B), and did not bind to any of the sites identified on the Dock2 promoter (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by chromatin immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A

claim: Elmo1 is a previously unidentified direct target of TGFβ signaling via SMAD3.
source: These results indicated that Elmo1 is a previously unidentified direct target of TGFβ signaling via SMAD3.
evidence: Inferred from the ChIP data showing SMAD3 binding to the Elmo1 promoter

claim: Lentiviral infection of Tgfbr2 cKO CD34+ SCC cells with the full-length Tgfbr2 gene resulted in rescue of Tgfbr2 mRNA by more than 4000-fold.
source: Lentiviral infection of Tgfbr2 cKO CD34+ SCC cells with the full-length Tgfbr2 gene inserted into the pLVX-IRES-mCherry vector resulted in rescue of Tgfbr2 mRNA by more than 4000-fold (C–D)
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6C-D

claim: Rescued CD34+ SCC cells became sensitive to TGFβ treatment and phosphorylated SMAD2.
source: Rescued CD34+ SCC cells became sensitive to TGFβ treatment and phosphorylated SMAD2 (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6E

claim: Orthotopic transplantation of rescued CD34+ SCC cells resulted in a two-fold delay in tumor latency compared to Tgfbr2 cKO CD34+ SCC cells infected with the empty vector.
source: Orthotopic transplantation of rescued CD34+ SCC cells resulted in a two-fold delay in tumor latency compared to Tgfbr2 cKO CD34+ SCC cells infected with the empty vector (Figure 6—figure supplement 2)
evidence: Supported by transplantation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2

claim: Restoration of Tgfbr2 in Tgfbr2 cKO CD34+ SCCs dramatically reduced the frequency of mCherry+CD34+ CSCs from 6.5% to 2.5%.
source: Restoration of Tgfbr2 in Tgfbr2 cKO CD34+ SCCs dramatically reduced the frequency of mCherry+CD34+ CSCs from 6.5% to 2.5% (Figure 6F)
evidence: Supported by FACS data shown in Figure 6F

claim: Loss of TGFβ signaling is a requirement for CSC maintenance in transition zone carcinoma.
source: Restoration of Tgfbr2 in Tgfbr2 cKO CD34+ SCCs dramatically reduced the frequency of mCherry+CD34+ CSCs from 6.5% to 2.5% (Figure 6F), demonstrating that loss of TGFβ signaling is a requirement for CSC maintenance in transition zone carcinoma.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that restoring TGFβ signaling reduces CSC frequency

claim: Rescue of Tgfbr2 abolished Elmo1 mRNA expression in YFP+mCherry+ cells isolated from tumors generated from Tgfbr2 cKO CD34+ SCC cells infected with full-length Tgfbr2 compared to YFP+mCherry-CD34+ cells isolated from the same tumor.
source: Importantly, rescue of Tgfbr2 abolished Elmo1 mRNA expression in YFP+mCherry+ cells isolated from tumors generated from Tgfbr2 cKO CD34+ SCC cells infected with full-length Tgfbr2 compared to YFP+mCherry-CD34+ cells isolated from the same tumor (Figure 6H)
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6H

claim: The RAC-activating GEF Elmo1 is a novel target of TGFβ repression.
source: Importantly, rescue of Tgfbr2 abolished Elmo1 mRNA expression in YFP+mCherry+ cells isolated from tumors generated from Tgfbr2 cKO CD34+ SCC cells infected with full-length Tgfbr2 compared to YFP+mCherry-CD34+ cells isolated from the same tumor (Figure 6H), confirming that the RAC-activating GEF Elmo1 is a novel target of TGFβ repression.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that restoring TGFβ signaling abolishes Elmo1 expression

claim: ELMO1 was expressed in 5 of the 15 of anorectal tumors tested.
source: We found that ELMO1 was expressed in 5 of the 15 of anorectal tumors tested (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data summarized in Table 1

claim: Loss of phosphorylated SMAD2 within the tumor tissue was observed in 5 out of 6 invasive SCC.
source: Concomitant with this expression was a corresponding loss of phosphorylated SMAD2 within the tumor tissue in 5 out of 6 invasive SCC (Table 1 and Figure 7C–E, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Table 1 and Figure 7C-E, Figure 7—figure supplement 1

claim: None of the early stage tumors tested (anal intraepithelial neoplasia or SCC in situ) expressed ELMO1.
source: Interestingly, none of the early stage tumors tested (anal intraepithelial neoplasia or SCC in situ) expressed ELMO1
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data

claim: Early stage tumors stained strongly for nuclear phosphorylated SMAD2 similarly to normal anorectal mucosa.
source: Interestingly, none of the early stage tumors tested (anal intraepithelial neoplasia or SCC in situ) expressed ELMO1, and these specimens stained strongly for nuclear phosphorylated SMAD2 similarly to normal anorectal mucosa (Figure 7A–B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 7A-B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1

claim: Treatment of Tgfbr2 cKO CD34+ SCC cells with Elmo1 shRNA resulted in 40% (construct #1) or 50% (construct #2) reduction in endogenous Elmo1 mRNA levels, compared to cells infected with control shRNA (SH02).
source: Treatment of Tgfbr2 cKO CD34+ SCC cells with Elmo1 shRNA resulted in 40% (construct #1) or 50% (construct #2) reduction in endogenous Elmo1 mRNA levels, compared to cells infected with control shRNA (SH02) (Figure 8A).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 8A

claim: Knocking down Elmo1 in Tgfbr2 cKO CD34+ SCC cells affected their ability to migrate and close the wound.
source: We performed an in vitro wound healing assay to show that knocking down Elmo1 in Tgfbr2 cKO CD34+ SCC cells affected their ability to migrate and close the wound.
evidence: Supported by wound healing assay data shown in Figure 8D-E

claim: The effect of Elmo1 knockdown on cell migration was rescued when Elmo1 knockdown cells expressed the hairpin-resistant ELMO1* construct.
source: This effect was rescued when Elmo1 knockdown cells expressed the hairpin-resistant ELMO1* construct (Figure 8D–E and Video 1).
evidence: Supported by wound healing assay data shown in Figure 8D-E and Video 1

claim: The effect of Elmo1 knockdown in cell migration was not due to a difference in proliferation.
source: We confirmed that the effect in cell migration was not due to a difference in proliferation as measured by flow cytometry (Figure 8F).
evidence: Supported by cell proliferation assay data shown in Figure 8F

claim: Elmo1 knockdown does not affect the proportion of CSC CD34+YFP+mCherry+ cells analyzed by FACS.
source: Consistent with this result, we observed that Elmo1 knockdown does not affect the proportion of CSC CD34+YFP+mCherry+ cells analyzed by FACS (Control SH02: 4.1% compared to Elmo1 shRNA: 3.3%, Figure 9—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: Supported by FACS data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1A

claim: A dramatic reduction in RAC1 staining at the tumor-stroma border was observed in tumors with Elmo1 knockdown.
source: Consistent with a migration defect in vitro (Figure 8D), we observed a dramatic reduction in RAC1 staining at the tumor-stroma border in tumors with Elmo1 knockdown (Figure 9A–A')
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 9A-A'

claim: RAC1 staining was rescued in cells expressing the hairpin-resistant ELMO1* construct.
source: Consistent with a migration defect in vitro (Figure 8D), we observed a dramatic reduction in RAC1 staining at the tumor-stroma border in tumors with Elmo1 knockdown (Figure 9A–A'), which was rescued in cells expressing the hairpin-resistant ELMO1* construct (Figure 9A'').
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 9A''

claim: Elmo1 knockdown resulted in a significant reduction in mRNA expression of Snail, αSma, Vimentin, Zeb2 and Mmp9 in CD34+ cells isolated from Tgfbr2 cKO tumors.
source: Because RAC signaling plays a role in tumor invasion, we hypothesized that a number of markers of EMT and/or invasion would be altered upon Elmo1 knockdown, and indeed observed reduction in the mRNA expression of Snail, αSma, Vimentin, Zeb2 and Mmp9 in CD34+ cells isolated from Tgfbr2 cKO tumors infected with both Elmo1 shRNA constructs #1 and #2 compared to those infected with SH02 control (Figure 9B).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 9B

claim: The level of mRNA expression of invasive markers was restored or increased in the cells expressing the hairpin-resistant ELMO1* construct.
source: The level of mRNA expression of these genes was restored or increased in the cells expressing the hairpin-resistant ELMO1* construct (Figure 9—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 2B

claim: Elmo1 reduction alters localization of RAC in Tgfbr2-deficient SCC in vivo and reduces the expression of invasive markers in CD34+ CSCs.
source: These results indicate that Elmo1 reduction alters localization of RAC in Tgfbr2-deficient SCC in vivo and reduces the expression of invasive markers in CD34+ CSCs.
evidence: Inferred from the immunofluorescence and qPCR data showing reduced RAC1 localization and reduced invasive marker expression

claim: A dramatic overall reduction in the number of YFP+ cells in the lungs of mice orthotopically transplanted with Tgfbr2 cKO CD34+ cells infected with Elmo1 shRNA knockdown compared to those infected with SH02 control was observed (n = 6 mice in each condition).
source: We observed a dramatic overall reduction in the number of YFP+ cells in the lungs of mice orthotopically transplanted with Tgfbr2 cKO CD34+ cells infected with Elmo1 shRNA knockdown compared to those infected with SH02 control (n = 6 mice in each condition) (Figure 10A–B).
evidence: Supported by FACS analysis of lung cells shown in Figure 10A-B

claim: 1.4% YFP+ cells were detected in the lungs of mice transplanted with the SH02 control cells.
source: We detected 1.4% YFP+ cells in the lungs of mice transplanted with the SH02 control cells
evidence: Supported by FACS analysis of lung cells

claim: A dramatic reduction to 0.4% YFP+ cells in mice transplanted with the ELMO1 shRNA#1 was detected.
source: We detected 1.4% YFP+ cells in the lungs of mice transplanted with the SH02 control cells, whereas we detected a dramatic reduction to 0.4% YFP+ cells in mice transplanted with the ELMO1 shRNA#1
evidence: Supported by FACS analysis of lung cells

claim: No YFP+ cells were detected in the lungs of mice transplanted with ELMO1 shRNA #2.
source: We detected 1.4% YFP+ cells in the lungs of mice transplanted with the SH02 control cells, whereas we detected a dramatic reduction to 0.4% YFP+ cells in mice transplanted with the ELMO1 shRNA#1 and failed to detect any YFP+ cells in the lungs of mice transplanted with ELMO1 shRNA #2.
evidence: Supported by FACS analysis of lung cells

claim: YFP+ metastatic nodules were observed in mice transplanted with SH02 cells, but never in mice transplanted with Elmo1 shRNA-infected cells.
source: We serially sectioned and stained the whole lungs from additional tumor-bearing mice, and observed YFP+ metastatic nodules in mice transplanted with SH02 cells, but never in mice transplanted with Elmo1 shRNA-infected cells (Figure 10C)
evidence: Supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 10C

claim: Upregulation of the GEF ELMO1 is required for Tgfbr2-deficient SCC CD34+ CSCs to metastasize.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that upregulation of the GEF ELMO1 is required for Tgfbr2-deficient SCC CD34+ CSCs to metastasize.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Elmo1 knockdown dramatically reduces lung metastases

claim: Transition zones are distinct anatomical regions between two different types of epithelia, and function as stem cell niches in many regions of the body.
source: Transition zones are distinct anatomical regions between two different types of epithelia, and function as stem cell niches in many regions of the body (Runck et al., 2010; San Roman et al., 2011; Mcnairn and Guasch, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Runck et al., 2010; San Roman et al., 2011; Mcnairn and Guasch, 2011

claim: Populations of cells with stem cell characteristics have been found in the transition zones between the cornea and conjunctiva in the eye.
source: Populations of cells with stem cell characteristics, such as label-retention and self-renewal, and expression of stem cell markers such as the cell surface glycoprotein CD34, have been found in the transition zones between the cornea and conjunctiva in the eye (Zieske, 1994; Cotsarelis et al., 1989)
evidence: Supported by citations to Zieske, 1994; Cotsarelis et al., 1989

claim: Populations of cells with stem cell characteristics have been found in the transition zones between the esophagus and the stomach.
source: Populations of cells with stem cell characteristics, such as label-retention and self-renewal, and expression of stem cell markers such as the cell surface glycoprotein CD34, have been found in the transition zones between the cornea and conjunctiva in the eye (Zieske, 1994; Cotsarelis et al., 1989), between the esophagus and the stomach (Kalabis et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citation to Kalabis et al., 2008

claim: Populations of cells with stem cell characteristics have been found in the transition zones between the endocervix and ectocervix.
source: Populations of cells with stem cell characteristics, such as label-retention and self-renewal, and expression of stem cell markers such as the cell surface glycoprotein CD34, have been found in the transition zones between the cornea and conjunctiva in the eye (Zieske, 1994; Cotsarelis et al., 1989), between the esophagus and the stomach (Kalabis et al., 2008), between the endocervix and ectocervix (Elson et al., 2000; Herfs et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citations to Elson et al., 2000; Herfs et al., 2012

claim: Populations of cells with stem cell characteristics have been found in the transition zones between the mesothelium and oviductal epithelium of the ovary.
source: Populations of cells with stem cell characteristics, such as label-retention and self-renewal, and expression of stem cell markers such as the cell surface glycoprotein CD34, have been found in the transition zones between the cornea and conjunctiva in the eye (Zieske, 1994; Cotsarelis et al., 1989), between the esophagus and the stomach (Kalabis et al., 2008), between the endocervix and ectocervix (Elson et al., 2000; Herfs et al., 2012), between the mesothelium and oviductal epithelium of the ovary (Flesken-Nikitin et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citation to Flesken-Nikitin et al., 2013

claim: Populations of cells with stem cell characteristics have been found in the transition zones between the anal canal and the rectum.
source: Populations of cells with stem cell characteristics, such as label-retention and self-renewal, and expression of stem cell markers such as the cell surface glycoprotein CD34, have been found in the transition zones between the cornea and conjunctiva in the eye (Zieske, 1994; Cotsarelis et al., 1989), between the esophagus and the stomach (Kalabis et al., 2008), between the endocervix and ectocervix (Elson et al., 2000; Herfs et al., 2012), between the mesothelium and oviductal epithelium of the ovary (Flesken-Nikitin et al., 2013) and between the anal canal and the rectum (Runck et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Runck et al., 2010

claim: Transition zones are uniquely susceptible to carcinogenesis, and the resulting tumors are typically highly malignant and associated with poor prognosis.
source: Transition zones are uniquely susceptible to carcinogenesis, and the resulting tumors are typically highly malignant and associated with poor prognosis (San Roman et al., 2011; Mcnairn and Guasch, 2011; Flesken-Nikitin et al., 2013; Grodsky, 1961).
evidence: Supported by citations to San Roman et al., 2011; Mcnairn and Guasch, 2011; Flesken-Nikitin et al., 2013; Grodsky, 1961

claim: As many as 86% of esophageal tumors arise in association with Barrett's esophagus at the esophageal-gastric junction.
source: As many as 86% of esophageal tumors arise in association with Barrett's esophagus at the esophageal-gastric junction (Trudgill et al., 2003; Yamamoto et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Trudgill et al., 2003; Yamamoto et al., 2016

claim: The transition zone in the ovary was recently shown to be acutely sensitive to oncogenic transformation.
source: The transition zone in the ovary was recently shown to be acutely sensitive to oncogenic transformation (Flesken-Nikitin et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Flesken-Nikitin et al., 2013

claim: Cervical cancers arise at the transition between the columnar epithelium of the endocervix and the squamous epithelium of the ectocervix.
source: Cervical cancers arise at the transition between the columnar epithelium of the endocervix and the squamous epithelium of the ectocervix (Elson et al., 2000; Herfs et al., 2012; Petignat and Roy, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Elson et al., 2000; Herfs et al., 2012; Petignat and Roy, 2007

claim: Highly malignant squamous cell carcinomas (SCC) develop between the stratified epithelium of the anal canal and the simple epithelia of the rectum.
source: Highly malignant squamous cell carcinomas (SCC) develop between the stratified epithelium of the anal canal and the simple epithelia of the rectum (Grodsky, 1961; Kim et al., 2013; Guasch et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Grodsky, 1961; Kim et al., 2013; Guasch et al., 2007

claim: Deregulated TGFβ signaling seems to be a hallmark of aggressive transition zone cancers.
source: Deregulated TGFβ signaling seems to be a hallmark of aggressive transition zone cancers.
evidence: Based on multiple observations in different transition zone cancers described in the manuscript

claim: In cervical cancer, mutations or loss of TGFβ downstream effectors SMAD2 and SMAD4 are common.
source: In cervical cancer, mutations or loss of TGFβ downstream effectors SMAD2 and SMAD4 are common (Maliekal et al., 2003)
evidence: Supported by citation to Maliekal et al., 2003

claim: Loss of nuclear SMAD2 and SMAD4 is associated with poor survival in cervical cancer.
source: In cervical cancer, mutations or loss of TGFβ downstream effectors SMAD2 and SMAD4 are common (Maliekal et al., 2003), and loss of nuclear SMAD2 and SMAD4 is associated with poor survival (Kloth et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kloth et al., 2008

claim: In genital SCC, TGFβ receptor (TGFβRII) protein expression is decreased and loss of phosphorylated SMAD2 is observed, even at early stages.
source: In genital SCC, TGFβ receptor (TGFβRII) protein expression is decreased and loss of phosphorylated SMAD2 is observed, even at early stages, suggesting that loss of TGFβ signaling may be an early event in carcinogenesis (Guasch et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Guasch et al., 2007

claim: Loss of TGFβ signaling may be an early event in carcinogenesis of genital SCC.
source: In genital SCC, TGFβ receptor (TGFβRII) protein expression is decreased and loss of phosphorylated SMAD2 is observed, even at early stages, suggesting that loss of TGFβ signaling may be an early event in carcinogenesis (Guasch et al., 2007).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that TGFβ signaling loss occurs at early stages, supported by citation to Guasch et al., 2007

claim: Many epithelia develop normally despite the loss of a component of the TGFβ signaling pathway.
source: Many epithelia develop normally despite the loss of a component of the TGFβ signaling pathway (Guasch et al., 2007; Muñoz et al., 2006; Biswas et al., 2004; Padua and Massagué, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Guasch et al., 2007; Muñoz et al., 2006; Biswas et al., 2004; Padua and Massagué, 2009

claim: Tumorigenesis occurs rapidly when epithelia lacking TGFβ signaling are exposed to carcinogens.
source: However, tumorigenesis occurs rapidly when these epithelia are exposed to carcinogens (Biswas et al., 2004)
evidence: Supported by citation to Biswas et al., 2004

claim: Within the gastric transition zone, loss of SMAD3 results in invasive carcinoma.
source: Within the gastric transition zone, loss of SMAD3 (Nam et al., 2012) or BMP signaling (Bleuming et al., 2007) results in invasive carcinoma.
evidence: Supported by citation to Nam et al., 2012

claim: Within the gastric transition zone, loss of BMP signaling results in invasive carcinoma.
source: Within the gastric transition zone, loss of SMAD3 (Nam et al., 2012) or BMP signaling (Bleuming et al., 2007) results in invasive carcinoma.
evidence: Supported by citation to Bleuming et al., 2007

claim: Mice with a neuronal-specific deletion of Tgfbr1 develop spontaneous periorbital and perianal SCC.
source: Mice with a neuronal-specific deletion of Tgfbr1 develop spontaneous periorbital and perianal SCC (Honjo et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Honjo et al., 2007

claim: The backskin of mice lacking Tgfbr2 in all Keratin 14-expressing (K14+) progenitors of the stratified epithelia is morphologically normal.
source: The backskin of mice lacking Tgfbr2 in all Keratin 14-expressing (K14+) progenitors of the stratified epithelia is morphologically normal, but these mice develop spontaneous SCC in cervical and anorectal transition zones (Guasch et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Guasch et al., 2007

claim: Mice lacking Tgfbr2 in all Keratin 14-expressing (K14+) progenitors develop spontaneous SCC in cervical and anorectal transition zones.
source: The backskin of mice lacking Tgfbr2 in all Keratin 14-expressing (K14+) progenitors of the stratified epithelia is morphologically normal, but these mice develop spontaneous SCC in cervical and anorectal transition zones (Guasch et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Guasch et al., 2007

claim: RHO and RAC-guanine triphosphatases (GTPases) are small G proteins (21–25 kDa), and belong to the RAS superfamily.
source: RHO and RAC-guanine triphosphatases (GTPases) are small G proteins (21–25 kDa), and belong to the RAS superfamily (Parri et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Parri et al., 2010

claim: RHO and RAC GTPases act as molecular switches to elicit rapid changes in cell shape, polarity, and migratory ability in response to external cues.
source: They act as molecular switches to elicit rapid changes in cell shape, polarity, and migratory ability in response to external cues (Parri et al., 2010; Vega and Ridley, 2008; Sadok et al., 2014; Alan and Lundquist, 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to Parri et al., 2010; Vega and Ridley, 2008; Sadok et al., 2014; Alan and Lundquist, 2013

claim: RHO and RAC GTPases are major players in malignant cell invasion.
source: They act as molecular switches to elicit rapid changes in cell shape, polarity, and migratory ability in response to external cues (Parri et al., 2010; Vega and Ridley, 2008; Sadok et al., 2014; Alan and Lundquist, 2013) and are major players in malignant cell invasion.
evidence: Based on established knowledge in the field

claim: RAC exists in an inactive form, bound to GDP, and in an active form, bound to GTP.
source: RAC exists in an inactive form, bound to GDP, and in an active form, bound to GTP (Parri et al., 2010; Sadok et al., 2014; Laurin and Cote, 2014; Lazer and Katzav, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Parri et al., 2010; Sadok et al., 2014; Laurin and Cote, 2014; Lazer and Katzav, 2011

claim: Guanine exchange factors (GEFs) are required to promote the active, GTP-bound form of RAC.
source: Guanine exchange factors (GEFs) are required to promote the active, GTP-bound form of RAC, and GTPase activating proteins (GAPs) return RAC to its inactive, GDP-bound state (Parri et al., 2010; Vega and Ridley, 2008; Sadok et al., 2014; Laurin and Cote, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Parri et al., 2010; Vega and Ridley, 2008; Sadok et al., 2014; Laurin and Cote, 2014

claim: GTPase activating proteins (GAPs) return RAC to its inactive, GDP-bound state.
source: Guanine exchange factors (GEFs) are required to promote the active, GTP-bound form of RAC, and GTPase activating proteins (GAPs) return RAC to its inactive, GDP-bound state (Parri et al., 2010; Vega and Ridley, 2008; Sadok et al., 2014; Laurin and Cote, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Parri et al., 2010; Vega and Ridley, 2008; Sadok et al., 2014; Laurin and Cote, 2014

claim: More than 70 GEFs have been described, which act downstream of many signaling pathways, including growth factor receptors, integrins, cadherins, and cytokine receptors.
source: More than 70 GEFs have been described, which act downstream of many signaling pathways, including growth factor receptors, integrins, cadherins, and cytokine receptors (Parri et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Parri et al., 2010

claim: ELMO proteins form a complex with DOCK proteins that serves as a GEF for RAC proteins.
source: ELMO proteins form a complex with DOCK proteins that serves as a GEF for RAC proteins.
evidence: Based on established knowledge in the field

claim: The ELMO-DOCK complex plays important roles in chemotaxis, phagocytosis, neurite outgrowth, and cancer cell invasion.
source: This complex plays important roles in chemotaxis, phagocytosis, neurite outgrowth, and cancer cell invasion (Laurin and Cote, 2014; Côté and Vuori, 2007; Gumienny et al., 2001; Grimsley et al., 2004; Brugnera et al., 2002; Jarzynka et al., 2007; Sai et al., 2008; Li et al., 1706; Komander et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Laurin and Cote, 2014; Côté and Vuori, 2007; Gumienny et al., 2001; Grimsley et al., 2004; Brugnera et al., 2002; Jarzynka et al., 2007; Sai et al., 2008; Li et al., 1706; Komander et al., 2008

claim: Subsets of long-lived tumor-initiating stem cells or cancer stem cells (CSCs) are often resistant to cancer therapies and thus may be responsible for tumor recurrence.
source: Subsets of long-lived tumor-initiating stem cells or cancer stem cells (CSCs) are often resistant to cancer therapies and thus may be responsible for tumor recurrence (Clevers, 2011; Malanchi et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Clevers, 2011; Malanchi et al., 2012

claim: CSCs sustain tumor growth through their ability to self-renew and to generate differentiated progeny.
source: They sustain tumor growth through their ability to self-renew and to generate differentiated progeny, and they may play a role in metastasis (Clevers, 2011; Malanchi et al., 2012; Oskarsson et al., 2014; Chaffer and Weinberg, 2011; Charafe-Jauffret et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Clevers, 2011; Malanchi et al., 2012; Oskarsson et al., 2014; Chaffer and Weinberg, 2011; Charafe-Jauffret et al., 2010

claim: CSCs may play a role in metastasis.
source: They sustain tumor growth through their ability to self-renew and to generate differentiated progeny, and they may play a role in metastasis (Clevers, 2011; Malanchi et al., 2012; Oskarsson et al., 2014; Chaffer and Weinberg, 2011; Charafe-Jauffret et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Clevers, 2011; Malanchi et al., 2012; Oskarsson et al., 2014; Chaffer and Weinberg, 2011; Charafe-Jauffret et al., 2010
